The paper uses: (a) if the functional j-invariant is non-zero there is exactly one additive fiber; (b) II+I₉ does not occur; (c) a III fiber occurs together with a semistable fiber I_m, 6≤m≤9, only as III+I₆ and III+I₈; (d) II* and I₃* whose two other rational fibers are smooth force exactly one further singular fiber, of type I₁, and so does IV*+E+I₃; (e) with j≠0, III* occurs only in Lang's Case 7, with singular fibers III*+I₁+I₁; (f) with j=0 there are at most three singular fibers, and a non-reduced fiber forces the remaining rational fiber to be smooth (Lang 2000, p. 5829); (g) the normal forms of Lang's Cases 2A, 5A, 5D, 7, 13A and 14 quoted in the proofs of Theorems 10.4 and 10.5.
items.note: W. Lang, Configurations of singular fibres on rational elliptic surfaces in characteristic two, Comm. Algebra 28 (2000), 5813–5836, is a prerequisite and was not re-derived. The finite checks for /104–/114 confirm the eleven equations (discriminants, j-invariants, smooth fibers), not the exhaustiveness in (a)–(g).

items.name: Additive reduction from c₄, and Tate's algorithm
items.statement: For a Weierstrass equation over a DVR with perfect residue field whose reduction is singular (Δ in the maximal ideal), the reduction is additive if and only if c₄ lies in the maximal ideal (Deligne, Formulaire, Proposition 5.1); in characteristic 2, c₄=a₁⁴. From a minimal Weierstrass equation, Tate's algorithm computes the Kodaira type, the number of components and the splitness of the special fiber of the minimal regular model.
items.locator: proof of Proposition 10.3, p. 29; proof of Theorem 10.4, pp. 30–31
items.note: Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 4 plans reduction types, Kodaira types and Tate's algorithm over a DVR. The singular-reduction hypothesis is needed: a smooth supersingular fiber in characteristic 2 also has c₄=0 (sourceIssue E15).

items.name: Weierstrass curves, their invariants and changes of coordinates
items.statement: A Weierstrass curve over a commutative ring R is a tuple (a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄,a₆)∈R⁵, with invariants b₂,b₄,b₆,b₈,c₄,c₆, discriminant Δ, j-invariant j=c₄³/Δ when Δ is a unit, and the admissible changes of coordinates (u,r,s,t) acting on the coefficients.
items.note: Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/Weierstrass.lean:77 (WeierstrassCurve), :121 (c₄), :132 (Δ), :389 (j, defined as Δ′⁻¹·c₄³ under IsElliptic); VariableChange.lean:57.

items.name: Zeta functions and the Weil conjectures (as used)
items.statement: For X smooth proper over F_q, the zeta function Z(X,t)=exp(Σ_s N_s t^s/s) is rational (Dwork); the ℓ-adic cohomology H^i(X̄,Q_ℓ(j)) is finite-dimensional, with H^i(X̄,Q_ℓ(j))=H^i(X̄,Q_ℓ)⊗Q_ℓ(j); the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula gives Z(X,t)=∏_i det(1−t f_i)^{(−1)^{i+1}}, f_i the geometric Frobenius on H^i(X̄,Q_ℓ); Poincaré duality holds; and the eigenvalues of f_i are algebraic integers of absolute value q^{i/2} in every complex embedding (Deligne).
items.note: WeilConjectures WC.1 plans rationality and the point-count API, WC.2 Poincaré duality and WC.3 integrality and the Riemann hypothesis; the trace formula comes from the pinned point-counting source that WC.0 and EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.8 cite. Integrality holds for the untwisted f_i, not for all twists (sourceIssue E10).

items.name: Cycle class maps and base change
items.statement: For X smooth over a perfect field k there are cycle class maps CH^j(X)→H^{2j}(X,Q_ℓ(j)), compatible with base change to k̄ (the square (8)).
items.note: EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves EDC.3 plans cycle classes over perfect fields, including finite fields.

items.name: Brauer–Hasse–Noether sequence for ℚ
items.statement: The sequence 0→Br(ℚ)→⊕_v Br(ℚ_v)→ℚ/ℤ→0, v running over all places including the real one, is exact.
items.note: Tau Ceti ClassFieldTheory Layer 10 plans this sequence for number fields, with the real place.

items.name: Pic(ℤ)=0 and Br(ℤ)=0
items.statement: Pic(Spec ℤ)=0, since ℤ is a principal ideal domain, and Br(Spec ℤ)=0: Br(ℤ) injects into Br(ℚ) because Spec ℤ is regular of dimension one; its classes are unramified at every prime because Br(ℤ_p)=Br(F_p)=0; so by the Brauer–Hasse–Noether sequence (/203) such a class is determined by its real invariant, which the sum formula forces to vanish.
items.locator: proof of Proposition 5.5, pp. 15–16; Theorem 5.6 applied to R=ℤ
items.note: The étale Brauer group of a scheme and the injection Br(X)→Br(K) for regular integral X of dimension one are not planned; /203 supplies the field sequence.

items.name: Kummer sequences over a base
items.statement: For S=Spec R, the Kummer sequence 0→μ₂→G_m→G_m→0 on the fppf site gives exact sequences 0→R^×/R^{×2}→H¹(S,μ₂)→Pic(S)[2]→0 and Pic(S)→Pic(S)→H²(S,μ₂)→Br(S)→Br(S), the unlabelled maps being multiplication by 2. In particular Pic(S)=Br(S)=0 gives H¹(S,μ₂)=R^×/R^{×2} and H²(S,μ₂)=0.
items.note: SchemeAndStackFoundations SF.2 owns fppf and étale cohomology of schemes; this computation is not stated there.

items.name: Tsen's theorem
items.statement: For an algebraically closed field k, the field k(t) is C₁, so Br(k(t))=0. Consequently, for a proper curve C over k(t) with H⁰(C,O_C)=k(t), every k(t)-point of Pic_{C/k(t)} comes from a line bundle on C.
items.note: The paper applies Tsen's theorem to F₂(t), where it fails (sourceIssue E13); the repair in /94 uses it over F̄₂(t) only.

items.name: Classification of indefinite unimodular lattices
items.statement: An indefinite unimodular lattice is determined up to isometry by its rank, signature and parity (Milnor–Husemoller, Chapter II, Theorem 5.3). In particular an even unimodular lattice of signature (1,9) is isometric to U⊕E₈(−1).
items.note: Tau Ceti has the hyperbolic plane, E₈ as D₈⁺ and unimodularity (TauCeti/LinearAlgebra/IntegralLattice/Examples.lean:81, hyperbolicPlane; RootLattice/D8Plus/Basic.lean:164, d8PlusLattice; Unimodular.lean:56, IsUnimodular) but not the classification of indefinite forms; Tau Ceti GlobalQuadraticForms classifies rational quadratic forms, not lattices. /29 consumes it.

items.name: Norm maps on Picard groups
items.statement: For a finite locally free morphism π:X′→X of constant rank n there is a norm homomorphism N:Pic(X′)→Pic(X), compatible with base change, with N(π*L)≅L^{⊗n} for every line bundle L on X (EGA II, §6.5).
items.locator: proof of Lemma 1.1, p. 5; proof of Lemma 8.4, p. 23
items.note: Used for the torsion of the descent obstruction in Lemma 1.1 (/2) and for Lemma 8.4 (/84).

items.name: Relatively minimal regular models and jacobian fibrations
items.statement: Let B be a regular curve over a field, or the spectrum of a DVR, with function field K, and C a regular proper curve over K with H⁰(C,O_C)=K and H¹(C,O_C) of dimension one. C has a unique relatively minimal regular proper model S→B. Its jacobian — the elliptic curve Pic⁰_{C/K}, or in the quasi-elliptic case the regular compactification of the twisted form Pic⁰_{C/K} of G_a — has a unique relatively minimal regular model with a section, the jacobian fibration J→B.
items.note: Lichtenbaum and Shafarevich for minimal models; /71, /75 and /81 use the output.

items.name: Enriques reducibility theorem (as used)
items.statement: (Lang 1983, Theorem 4.1) Let φ:Y→P¹ be a genus-one fibration of an Enriques surface over an algebraically closed field. Every divisor class of degree two on the fibers contains, modulo vertical classes and multiples of a half-fiber, an integral curve R̃ with R̃²∈{0,−2}.
items.note: W. Lang, On Enriques surfaces in characteristic p. I, Math. Ann. 265 (1983), 45–65; stated as the paper uses it in /137 and /141.

items.name: Representability of the relative Picard functor (Artin)
items.statement: (Artin 1969, Theorem 7.3) For f:𝔜→Spec R flat, proper, of finite presentation and cohomologically flat in dimension zero, the fppf sheafification of A↦Pic(𝔜⊗_R A) is representable by a group algebraic space locally of finite presentation over R.
items.note: /49 and /50 specialize it to Enriques families with Ekedahl–Hyland–Shepherd-Barron, Corollary 4.3.

items.name: Subgroups of the Picard functor and torsors under the Cartier dual (Raynaud)
items.statement: (Raynaud 1970, Proposition 6.2.1) Let f:𝔜→S be flat, proper and of finite presentation with f_*O=O, and P⊂Pic_{𝔜/S} a finite locally free commutative subgroup scheme with Cartier dual G=Hom(P,G_m). The inclusion corresponds to a global section of R¹f_*(G_𝔜); by the five-term sequence (2) it comes from a G-torsor over 𝔜 exactly when its image in H²(S,G) vanishes, and such torsors are unique up to pullbacks of G-torsors over S.
items.note: /55–/60 build the canonical coverings of Proposition 5.4 from it.

The cited prerequisites (Lang 2000, Lang 1983, Cossec–Dolgachev, Ekedahl–Shepherd-Barron, Liu–Lorenzini–Raynaud, Fontaine 1993) were not re-read; their statements enter as the items /189–/212 and the earlier items that cite them.

summary: Schröer proves that there is no smooth proper family of Enriques surfaces over ℤ (Theorem 5.1). Over ℤ the Picard scheme of such a family would be constant (Proposition 5.5, using Minkowski, Br(ℤ) = 0 and Fontaine's bound on the Hodge numbers of varieties with good reduction everywhere); its fiber over F₂ would be non-exceptional (it lifts to ℤ/4ℤ); and no non-exceptional Enriques surface over F₂ has constant Picard scheme (Theorem 15.1). That last theorem rests on descent of curves and fibrations from F̄₂ (Theorem 5.6), a count of 25 rational points (Corollary 7.3), the transfer of constant Picard scheme to rational jacobian surfaces (Theorem 9.1), the classification of eleven Weierstrass equations over F₂[t] (Theorems 10.4–10.5), and a combinatorial elimination of fiber configurations (§§11–14) that uses Nikulin's discriminant forms. The atlas has no Enriques or elliptic surfaces, no genus-one fibrations and no Picard schemes of proper schemes over a field; it plans Tate's algorithm, surface intersection theory, the Weil conjectures and cycle classes, and Tau Ceti has the discriminant-form and overlattice library. 212 items (16 library, 12 planned, 184 missing) are routed to nine routes: a new roadmap for Enriques surfaces and the nonexistence proof, Part IIs of NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties (genus-one fibrations and rational elliptic surfaces), AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry (numerical Picard groups and contraction descent) and SmallRamificationAndAbelianVarietyBaseCases (low-degree Hodge obstructions), and sources for R07.1, WC.7, IG.0, A0-extension and SF.1–SF.2. Seventeen mistakes are recorded, including a gap in the proof of Proposition 5.5 (the canonical covers over ℤ[1/2] and over W(F̄₂) are compared without their twists) and the false claim Br(F₂(t)) = 0 in Proposition 9.3; both are repaired.

routes.title: Algebraic moduli and representability for arithmetic geometry, Part II: numerical Picard groups and contraction descent
routes.reason: A0-extension supplies relative Pic⁰ representability for arithmetic applications, not the numerical Picard local system of arbitrary proper schemes or descent of contractions. This extends that direction without rebuilding Picard representability.
routes.brief: Start from Algebraic moduli and representability for arithmetic geometry (AlgebraicModuliForArithmeticGeometry), especially A0-extension, and Scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.1,SF.2,SF.5). Construct Pic^τ and Num for arbitrary proper schemes over a field, including nonreduced and disconnected schemes; expose geometric base change, Galois action, numerical equivalence, torsion obstructions and norm maps. Prove the positive-power descent criterion with a numerically trivial twist, then Theorem 1.3: constant Num descends geometric contractions with projective target; treat purely inseparable descent separately without the constantness assumption. Prove Theorem 2.1 for contractions of smooth proper surfaces: component-graph descent, the geometrically-reduced edge-label assertion, and pure inseparability of residue fields of reducible fibers. Import surface intersections, not their reconstruction. Give each definition an API and at least three tests; include P¹_C/R with permuted numerical components, d=0 as a forbidden criterion, and projectivity versus arbitrary proper targets. The Enriques roadmap consumes these general theorems; it must not own a duplicate Picard theory. Add the killed-by-two numerical-class lift /183 as a sheaf-quotient construction. Import rigidified Picard descent from A0-extension and relative ampleness from R09.1/R09.3; the Enriques consumer owns the local-projectivity application.

routes.title: Néron models and semistable abelian varieties, Part II: genus-one fibrations and rational elliptic surfaces
routes.reason: R11.2/R11.4 provide Néron special fibers and degeneration interfaces; they do not classify regular genus-one torsor surfaces, rational elliptic surfaces or their F₂ configurations. EllipticCurves Layer 4 supplies the planned Tate algorithm and must remain its owner.
routes.brief: Build on Néron models and semistable abelian varieties (NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties:R11.2,R11.4), Elliptic curves (tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/EllipticCurves, Layer 4), and Scheme, stack, cohomology and intersection foundations (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3–SF.5). Cover regular minimal genus-one models, elliptic versus quasielliptic generic fibers, fiber multiplicities versus reduced and indecomposable divisors, geometric Kodaira types and finite-field nonsplit I₁/I₂ forms. Import the Tate algorithm, not a second algorithm. Prove the excellent-DVR isogeny theorem 8.1, extension-count corollary and special F₂ isomorphism; use Liu–Lorenzini–Raynaud 6.6 only with algebraically closed residue field. Construct the degree-bounded two-chart Weierstrass model of a smooth rational Jacobian. End with Theorem 9.4's precisely conditioned Picard-constancy criterion and Theorems 10.4/10.5: eight nonzero-j and three zero-j models under constant Picard and at most one rational semistable/supersingular fiber. Acquire Lang 2000 and verify its classification, including coordinate equivalence and Kodaira resolutions, before asserting completeness. Import Tau Ceti's IntegralLattices implementation for discriminants; separately prove its geometric lattice realization. Test the five F₂ curves, all 11 equation invariants, the degree-two I₁ exception, and the distinction between split component graph and split nodes. Also cover the general inputs the proofs use, each as its own node: the Kodaira–Néron classification of fibers (/189) and Szydło's schematic fibers over non-closed fields (/190); the canonical bundle formula (/191) and tame versus wild multiple fibers (/192); relatively minimal regular models and jacobian fibrations, elliptic and quasi-elliptic (/209); the invariants of rational elliptic surfaces (/196) and quasi-elliptic fibrations in characteristic 2 (/197); Lang's theorem on torsors over finite fields (/193), twisted forms of P¹ (/194), isogeny invariance of point counts (/195) and Tsen's theorem over algebraically closed constants (/206); and Lang's 2000 classification in the form the paper uses it (/198), from the source itself.

routes.title: Small ramification and the base cases for Serre modularity, Part II: low-degree Hodge obstructions
routes.reason: R25.3 is explicitly the everywhere-good-reduction obstruction for abelian varieties. A K3 application needs Fontaine 1993's higher-cohomology Hodge-vanishing theorem, not an enlargement by analogy.
routes.brief: Begin beyond Small ramification and the base cases for Serre modularity (SmallRamificationAndAbelianVarietyBaseCases:R25.1–R25.3), importing its discriminant and ramification methods. Import Finite flat group schemes and integral p-adic Hodge theory (FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory:R07.1,R07.3,R07.6) and the atlas's p-adic comparison owners rather than recreating their group schemes or comparison functors. Acquire and decompose Fontaine 1993 completely. The precise endpoint is: for proper smooth X/Q with good reduction over W(F_pbar) at every prime p, H^j(X,Ω_X^i)=0 for i≠j and i+j≤3. Retain the first remark after Theorem 1, which permits these local unramified models; a global Z-model hypothesis would not suffice for Schröer's proof as written. Derive the K3 obstruction from h^{2,0}=1. Keep construction of canonical Enriques covers and their twisting/comparison in the Enriques consumer, not here. Test the strict degree bound, a smooth projective-space example, and the difference between potentially good reduction after ramification and good reduction over the specified Witt ring. State all torsion-crystalline and small-ramification ranges, especially at 2; do not apply e<p−1 dyadically. This consumer now supplies projective scheme models over each Z_p in /63, which meets Fontaine Theorem 1 directly; retain remark(a) as the more general source contract.

routes.reason: The rank-two Oort–Tate construction and classification are a concrete additional source for the existing finite-flat classification/fiber/duality stage. Reuse the pinned affine finite-locally-free and Cartier-duality infrastructure; add only the missing rank-two classification and compatibility. The correct coordinate law has a minus sign. No reviewed R07.1 row was present in the inspected audit, so absence of a row is not evidence that all finite-flat theory is absent.

These are geometric worked realizations of the existing zeta/trace machinery: base-defined algebraic cycles yield scalar Frobenius, hence polynomial counts and the 25-point surface instance. Import WC.1–WC.3, cycle classes and smooth-proper hypotheses. Do not create another cohomology, zeta-function or Weil-conjecture roadmap.

routes.title: Enriques surfaces and nonexistence over the integers

routes.brief: Construct Enriques surfaces and flat proper finitely presented algebraic-space families, not only scheme families. Final endpoints are Schröer 5.1, no Enriques family over Z, and 15.1, no nonexceptional Enriques surface over F₂ with constant FULL Picard scheme. Import NumericalPicardAndContractionDescent for general descent; GenusOneFibrationsAndRationalEllipticSurfaces for Jacobians, Kodaira types and the 11-model classification; EverywhereGoodReductionAndLowDegreeHodgeNumbers for Fontaine's K3 obstruction; FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory:R07.1 for Oort–Tate; WeilConjectures:WC.7 for point counts; SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4–SF.5 for deformation and intersection foundations; and the BUILT tauceti:Completed/IntegralLattices for discriminant forms and overlattices. Cover the three characteristic-two types, canonical torsors and twists, conductrix/exceptionality, the no-W₂-lift input, and constant-Picard descent of line bundles, rational (-2)-curves and genus-one fibrations. Prove the geometric Num≅U⊕E₈(-1) comparison rather than rebuilding E₈. Implement the explicit four-twist comparison in item /63 before assembling Proposition 5.5 or 5.1: use Num-only finite-field counts and henselian lifting to obtain a cover over Z₂; express the Q₂ difference as (−1)^e2^a5^b; twist over Z[1/2] by (−1)^e2^a and over Z₂ by the étale model of 5^b. Supply the projective scheme models via /182–/186 before applying Fontaine. Import local-field Layers 1–2 and the existing strong Hensel declaration, not a second local-field theory. Descend Mordell–Weil sections using Tsen only over algebraically closed constants. Preserve the integral two-section branch of square 0 as well as−2; use the current v3 proof and its lattice matrices, not the superseded two-section argument. Prove all 15→8→0 configuration reductions, both ten-curve exclusions, simple and multiple III* separately, and Proposition 14.1 over arbitrary algebraically closed fields. Acquire Ekedahl–Shepherd-Barron, Cossec–Dolgachev and Lang's reducibility theorem before dependency closure. Every definition gets consumer-driven API, tests and a suggested Lean signature; formalization is a future design/implementation task. Include the classification of indefinite unimodular lattices (/207), which identifies Num with U⊕E₈(−1), and the Enriques reducibility theorem (/210) behind the two-section choices of §12.

routes.reason: A concrete finite-étale Galois-category application, importing the built number-field Minkowski declaration /180. No new discriminant proof or second fundamental-group construction.

Source-qualified rigidification and representation of Picard classes for algebraic spaces with a section. This supplies the existing higher-dimensional Picard direction; it does not create another Picard functor. Artin's representability of the relative Picard functor and Raynaud's correspondence between finite subgroups of Pic and torsors under the Cartier dual (/211–/212) are the general inputs of the same stage.

A concrete henselian section-lifting consequence for smooth separated algebraic spaces using a residue-preserving étale scheme chart. Import smooth algebra Hensel lifting, not the p-adic polynomial lemma as a geometric substitute. SF.2 owns fppf and étale cohomology of schemes; the paper also uses Pic(ℤ)=Br(ℤ)=0 and the Kummer sequences over a base (/204–/205), which belong there as computations.

sourceIssues.printed: The group scheme Num_{X/k} is constant if and only if there is an integer d ≥ 0 with the following property: For every invertible sheaf L on X̄ there is a numerically trivial invertible sheaf N on X̄ such that L^{⊗d} ⊗ N is the pullback of some invertible sheaf on X.
sourceIssues.reason: With d = 0 the property holds for every X (take N = O), so the 'if' direction would make every Num_{X/k} constant. It fails for X = P¹_ℂ regarded as a proper ℝ-scheme, whose geometric Num is ℤ² with complex conjugation exchanging the factors. The proof uses a subgroup of finite index, that is d ≥ 1. /2 states the corrected lemma.
